whoParas.text: Education For Development Association (EFDA) is an Ethiopian civil society organization working through community-based development in Oromia and Benishangul Gumuz.

Alongside standalone basic education projects run since our founding, EFDA uses education as an instrument of change in every other program — environmental protection, livelihoods, community health and peacebuilding — so that knowledge stays in the community long after a project ends.
Our education work spans Alternative Basic Education, quality improvement inside government primary schools, and the Speed School programme for children out of school for socioeconomic reasons.

meta.title: Enset in Woliso — a case study
meta.description: How EFDA cut the work of processing enset, with the Swiss Development Cooperation: from 8–10 women handling three stems a day to five people handling fifteen, and fermentation from three months to fifteen days.

enset.intro: Enset feeds more than 20 million Ethiopians. Processing it is done by hand, mostly by women, and takes months. Over eighteen months in Woliso, EFDA tried to change that — and wrote down what happened, including what did not work.

facts.v: Woliso town, South West Shewa, Oromia
Swiss Embassy / SDC — 65% of a CHF 310,277 budget
220 members across two producer enterprises, 91% women

enset.problemH2: A crop that survives famine, processed in a way that exhausts women.

problemParas.text: Enset — false banana — was domesticated in Ethiopia around ten thousand years ago. It tolerates drought, can be harvested at any time of year, and stores for long periods after fermenting. It is called the tree against hunger for good reason: it held through the famines that broke cereal crops.

But the processing has barely changed. Scraping the leaf sheath and pulverising the corm is manual work, and cultural norms put it on women. A group of eight to ten women would process three enset stems in a day, for about 100 birr each. The mixture then fermented in an earthen pit for two to three months, needing regular mixing, exposed to soil, flooding and spoiling microorganisms.
The result is a food with an odour that keeps it out of city shops, sold in a separate corner of the local market, returning very little to the people who grew and processed it.

enset.workH2: A demonstration centre, and machines that had to be proven first.

workParas.text: EFDA built the Centre for Enset Business Incubation at its Woliso facility — a washing sink, cutters, a dual-purpose scraping and pulverising machine from the Bako Agricultural Mechanization Centre, and squeezers sized for different volumes. The first squeezer worked at household scale but stayed labour-intensive for market quantities, so EFDA staff designed a larger one driven by a hydraulic jack.

Fermentation moved out of earthen pits and into sealed plastic barrels. Working with Arba Minch University, EFDA tested a starter culture and an additive made from banana, leaves, salt and moringa. Then a filtering step, new to enset processing, washes the fermented mixture to take out the fibre, and food-grade plastic replaces damp leaf sheaths for packaging.

Nothing was handed to anyone until it had been tested at the centre. Two producer enterprises were formed from women and unemployed young people with the fewest assets, trained in both the technique and the business, given equipment and start-up capital, and linked back to the centre for advice.

results.before: 8–10 women, three enset stems a day
two to three months in an earthen pit
results.after: as little as 15 days in a sealed barrel

results.before: a separate corner of the local market

enset.honestH2: Three things EFDA could not fix.

honestParas.text: Inflation. Cement, iron sheet, sand, gravel, wood and nails all rose through the project, and the renovation and the demonstration shade both depended on them. SDC accepted a budget revision and the removal of non-essential activities, which is the only reason the centre was finished.

Time. The pilot was planned for eighteen months. Each stage had to finish before the next could start, and the report says plainly that the period "was not realistic and it presented significant challenges".

Disease. Every time project staff met the community, enset disease came up, and it is the main reason enset cultivation is shrinking. EFDA states it is not in a position to address this — it needs national government and international attention — and commits only to keep advocating for it.

enset.nextH2: Three ways to reach producers who will never come to a centre.

nextParas.text: A household approach, where mobile operators bring portable equipment to the homestead for a fee. A centre-based approach, where an enterprise buys enset from nearby farmers, processes it and sells the product. Or a mixed approach, where households carry their stems to a centre for scraping and take the product home to ferment.

Beyond that, EFDA argues for disease-resistant varieties bred for different agro-ecologies, an agricultural extension system that stops treating enset as an afterthought to cereals, and portable machines simple enough to run on local knowledge.

meta.title: Strategy 2024–2028
meta.description: EFDA’s board-adopted strategic plan: four programme components, five strategic shifts, and what the organization intends to look like by 2028.

strategy.intro: In January 2024 EFDA adopted a five-year plan. It is unusually candid about what the organization does not yet do well, and specific about what it intends to change. This page is a summary of it.
strategy.baseH2: What the last period actually produced.
strategy.baseP: The plan opens with a review. These are its own figures for the period before it — the baseline everything that follows is measured against.

baseline.label: poor and marginalized women organized in self-help groups, in Ameya, Guto Gidda, Nekemte and Bokoji
young women from poor families completed a diploma or degree; 150 more were kept from dropping out
of Chato natural forest maintained under area closure, Horro Guduru Wollega
projects implemented across EFDA’s thematic areas in the period under review

strategy.compP: The plan organizes everything EFDA does into four components. Sustainable environment is deliberately not a separate programme — it is mainstreamed across all of them.

components.title: Socio-economic empowerment
components.text: Inequality, illiteracy and economic dependency fall hardest on women — in decision-making, in reproductive choice, in wages and in health. This is the component the self-help group work sits in.

components.title: Reducing women’s and girls’ health risks
components.text: Reproductive health education and psychosocial support, integrated into the economic work rather than run beside it. The plan credits it with local proclamations against harmful traditional practice, agreed with government, religious and traditional leaders.

components.title: Sustainable environment
components.text: Mainstreamed across every project rather than standing alone. Its concrete achievement is the Chato natural forest and 110 hectares of area closure in Horro Guduru Wollega.

components.title: Peacebuilding and conflict management
components.text: EFDA describes itself as "one of a few vibrant CSOs operating in the region", with over twenty years of grassroots presence — and says plainly that violent conflict has strained its operations and that it lacks the capacity and resources the emergency needs.

strategy.shiftP: The plan names five deliberate changes of direction. Three of them are admissions.

shifts.title: Strengthening capacity building
shifts.text: Of existing staff and of the board, through structured programmes rather than on the job.

shifts.title: Partnership, sustainability and documentation
shifts.text: Documentation today is "limited to quarterly and annual reports that are sent to donors". The plan commits to bulletins and news feeds so lessons are shared, not just reported.

shifts.title: A different approach to resource mobilization
shifts.text: "EFDA is totally dependent on donor funding which is limited to proposal development. As soliciting funding has become highly competitive, the organization needs to look for local resources to generating income."

shifts.title: Expanding and scaling up
shifts.text: EFDA’s vision allows it to work anywhere in Ethiopia, but "most of its past and present interventions are confined in Oromia National Regional State". The plan commits to new offices in two more Oromia zones and a base beyond the region.

shifts.title: A shift in who is served
shifts.text: Adding unemployed youth, internally displaced people, elderly women, and women and girls at risk of trafficking to the target groups.

strategy.targetP: The measurable commitments, as the plan states them.

targets.v: From five projects to eleven over five years — two new projects a year
New offices in two further Oromia zones, and a base outside the region
Growth of 30% a year. The plan states the rate but its sentence breaks off before naming a 2028 figure
75% of the yearly budget from donors, and retention of all existing donors who continue operating in Ethiopia
A 100% burn rate maintained throughout the plan period
The plan is reviewed at least every six months, with a midterm and a final evaluation

strategy.honestP: Strategic plans are usually written to impress. This one is worth reading because it is not. These are its own findings about EFDA.

admissions.text: The previous strategic plan, covering 2014 to 2019, "was not used as a tool to set priorities/goals" and "was not shared among staff".
There is no master budget aligned to the strategy, and no cost-sharing mechanism.
Finance and programme staff are too few, and segregation of duties has gaps "due to limited staff".
Procurement policy sits inside the human resources policy; the plan notes "it needs to be separate to meet donor’s requirements".
Publicity is poor, and there are "inadequate resources and capacity/skills to document EFDA works, outputs, outcomes/results".
Operational areas depend on which donors are interested, rather than on where need is greatest.

strategy.footH2: Fund a plan that names its own weaknesses.
